chmmc-2012-fall-team-02.title: Right triangle
chmmc-2012-fall-team-02.body:
$AB=3$, $BC=4$, $CA=5$, so the triangle is right-angled at $B$ with area $6$. Put $B=(0,0)$, $A=(0,3)$, $C=(4,0)$, $D=(0,2)$, $E=(1,0)$. Lines $AE$ and $CD$ meet at $F=\left(\frac25,\frac95\right)$. Then $[ECF]=\frac12\cdot3\cdot\frac95=\frac{27}{10}$ and $[ADF]=\frac12\cdot1\cdot\frac25=\frac15$. The difference is $\frac{27}{10}-\frac2{10}=\frac52$.

**Answer: $\frac52$**

chmmc-2012-fall-team-03.title: Complement graph
chmmc-2012-fall-team-03.body:
Take the graph simple. Its complement on $6$ vertices has $15-12=3$ edges, and a vertex of degree $d$ in $G$ has degree $5-d$ in the complement. A graph with $3$ edges has one of these shapes: a triangle (degrees $2,2,2,0,0,0$), a path of $3$ edges (degrees $1,2,2,1,0,0$), a star with $3$ edges ($3,1,1,1,0,0$), a path of $2$ edges plus a disjoint edge ($1,2,1,1,1,0$), or three disjoint edges ($1,1,1,1,1,1$). Complementing, the degree sequences of $G$ are $(3,3,3,5,5,5)$, $(4,3,3,4,5,5)$, $(2,4,4,4,5,5)$, $(4,3,4,4,4,5)$, $(4,4,4,4,4,4)$ respectively. An Eulerian path exists iff the graph is connected with at most two odd-degree vertices. The sequences with $0$ or $2$ odd vertices correspond to connected graphs (a vertex of degree $5$ is adjacent to everything; the sequence $(4,4,4,4,4,4)$ is the connected graph $K_{2,2,2}$), so they have Eulerian paths, while $(3,3,3,5,5,5)$ and $(3,3,4,4,5,5)$ have $6$ and $4$ odd vertices.

**Answer: $3,3,3,5,5,5$ and $3,3,4,4,5,5$**

chmmc-2012-fall-team-04.title: Cyclic quadrilateral
chmmc-2012-fall-team-04.body:
Since $\angle ABE=\angle ADE=90^\circ$, the points $A,B,D,E$ lie on the circle with diameter $AE$. The inscribed angles on chord $BD$ are equal: $\angle BAD=\angle BED=30^\circ$. In right triangle $ABC$ (right angle at $B$), $\angle BAC=30^\circ$, so $AC=\frac{AB}{\cos30^\circ}=\frac{\sqrt6}{\sqrt3/2}=2\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt2$**

chmmc-2012-fall-team-05.title: Count sequences
chmmc-2012-fall-team-05.body:
There are $3^5=243$ equally likely sequences. Subtract $2$ from each length: we need five numbers in $\{-1,0,1\}$ summing to $0$ (total $10-10=0$ after subtracting $2$ each). Count: all five $0$: $1$; one $+1$ and one $-1$: $5\cdot4=20$; two $+1$ and two $-1$: $\frac{5!}{2!2!1!}=30$. Total $51$. Probability $\frac{51}{243}=\frac{17}{81}$.

**Answer: $\frac{17}{81}$**

chmmc-2012-fall-team-06.title: Pigeonhole
chmmc-2012-fall-team-06.body:
There are only three colors, so among any $4$ socks two have the same color, and these form a matching pair. Three socks may all differ in color (one red, one blue, one green), so $3$ are not enough.

**Answer: 4**

chmmc-2012-fall-team-07.title: Unfold
chmmc-2012-fall-team-07.body:
Unfold two adjacent faces into a rectangle; the path is the diagonal. The three possible rectangles are $(1+2)\times3$, $(1+3)\times2$ and $(2+3)\times1$ with diagonals $\sqrt{18}$, $\sqrt{20}$, $\sqrt{26}$. The shortest is $\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt2$**

chmmc-2012-fall-team-08.title: Average palindrome
chmmc-2012-fall-team-08.body:
There are $9\cdot10^{14}$ palindromes (first $15$ digits, with $d_1\ne0$). If every one of the $30$ digit positions had average digit $4.5$, the average palindrome would be $4.5\cdot\frac{10^{30}-1}9=\frac{10^{30}-1}2$. The first and last digits actually average $5$ (not $4.5$), which adds $0.5\,(10^{29}+1)$. So the average palindrome is $\frac{10^{30}-1}2+\frac{10^{29}+1}2=\frac{11\cdot10^{29}}2=5.5\cdot10^{29}$ and the total is $9\cdot10^{14}\cdot5.5\cdot10^{29}=495\cdot10^{42}$.

**Answer: $495\times10^{42}$**

chmmc-2012-fall-team-08.title: Exact arithmetic
chmmc-2012-fall-team-08.body:
Summing digit $d_i$ with weight $10^{30-i}+10^{i-1}$ over all palindromes (digit $d_1$ totals $45\cdot10^{14}$, each other digit totals $405\cdot10^{13}$) with exact integer arithmetic gives $495\cdot10^{42}$.

**Answer: $495\times10^{42}$**

chmmc-2012-fall-team-09.title: Describe the residues
chmmc-2012-fall-team-09.body:
Write $n=4^km$ with $m$ odd (or $n=0$). If $x^2\equiv n\pmod{2^{12}}$ then $x=2^ky$ with $y$ odd and $y^2\equiv m\pmod{2^{12-2k}}$. Odd squares are $\equiv1\pmod8$, and every $m\equiv1\pmod8$ is an odd square modulo any power of $2$, so the nonzero residues are $n=4^km$ with $m\equiv1\pmod8$, $4^km<2^{12}$, $0\le k\le5$ (for $k=5$ only $m=1$, $n=1024$ occurs); also $n=0$. The sums over each $k$ are $1047040,260608,64000,14848,2560,1024$ for $k=0,\dots,5$, total $1390080=339\cdot4096+1536$. The remainder is $1536$.

**Answer: 1536**

chmmc-2012-fall-team-09.title: Direct computation
chmmc-2012-fall-team-09.body:
Computing $\{x^2\bmod4096:0\le x<4096\}$ and adding up the distinct residues gives $1390080\equiv1536\pmod{4096}$.

**Answer: 1536**
